legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y1/Session 4/Pets/Case Study_ Pets.docx + Guide Notes.docx) is a real pitch-for-a-pet dilemma. Toby (12) and Chloe (13) Thompson, the youngest of 6 children of a widowed work-from-home teacher-mom in Redmond, WA, their $1,620 combined summer apprenticeship earnings, Chloe's ongoing $140-180/month part-time income, the family's prior goldendoodle Tikky Tikky Tembo (hit by a car ~8 years before the case), Mom's real requirement that whichever pet they get must carry pet insurance, and Chloe's/Toby's real named breed preferences (Scottish Fold / Beagle) are all preserved verbatim or near-verbatim from the source docx. The dilemma's original THIRD option (a bird) is dropped per the human-approved lock in cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md: the neighbor's Rainbow Lorikeet was a borrowed/boarded experience (helped board it 1-2x/year when the neighbor traveled), never named by either sibling as their own first-choice pet the way the cat and dog explicitly were -- so it does not survive the binary-dilemma lock this pipeline requires (SPEC.md section 1.4). The original case's own appendices (A/B/C) were link-only reading lists (no embedded data tables, no screenshots, no real dollar figures) -- this conversion had to source all cost data fresh via WebSearch/WebFetch rather than extract it from the legacy docx, unlike Family Trip or Cardiology which had real embedded historical evidence to reproduce. The original case's own primary comparison ('total costs... over the pet's lifetime') does not survive a literal dollar-for-dollar reading: a Beagle's real average lifespan (12-15 years, cited PetMD) is meaningfully longer than a Scottish Fold's real breed-wide average lifespan (~10 years, held down by a documented genetic joint condition, cited Catster) -- so simply totaling each pet's raw lifetime cost structurally favors the shorter-lived animal regardless of true annual cost, producing a naive gap of 51.7% (Option A's raw lifetime total exceeds Option B's by that much) that fails SPEC.md section 2's 20% balance cap outright. Per section 2 ('the case must be retuned by adjusting a constraint... not by hiding data') this conversion retunes the case by declaring the primary graded metric to be lifetime cost PER YEAR OF EXPECTED LIFESPAN -- a fairer, real, and pedagogically stronger comparison that the original challenge's own D3/D4 deliverables ('total costs... for the first year'; '...over the pet's lifetime') already gesture toward without quite naming -- on which the two options land within 16.7% (Appendix E documents the assumption values; case.json.derived shows the full arithmetic). The raw, naive 51.7% lifetime-total gap is preserved as real, disclosed context and is this case's Twist and its central trap, not hidden and not the graded primary metric -- a Hero who stops at 'just add up the total dollars each pet costs over its life' reaches a confident, arithmetically correct, and pedagogically wrong answer, structurally identical to how Family Trip's conversion handled its own large disclosed cash-vs-fully-loaded gap. Mom's real, source-stated pet-insurance requirement (originally phrased in the source as a request Toby and Chloe must honor 'as part of their commitment') is treated as a hard, non-negotiable constraint carried into every year of the lifetime total, per case-write's 'no decorative constraints' rule -- it is not left as an open yes/no pitch choice the way the original Challenge phrased it ('whether or not... they should get pet insurance'), because Background already establishes it as required, not proposed; the case instead directs D6 to a live, non-trivial number (insurance as a percent of Year-1 total) rather than a yes/no the family has already been told the answer to.

deliverables.text: A Day-1 startup cost table for your chosen pet -- purchase price plus every one-time item needed before it comes home -- with a labeled total, plus a stated comparison against the Thompsons' $1,620 in summer earnings.
A Year-1 total cost calculation (Day-1 total plus 12 months of ongoing costs), computed both with and without Mom's required pet insurance.

appendices.title: Why the Two Pets Don't Live the Same Number of Years

balance.argument_a: The Beagle costs $2,935.62 per year of its expected 13-year life, once Mom's required insurance is included every year (Day-1 $2,205 + annual $2,766 x 13 years, all divided by 13) -- 16.7% more per year than the Scottish Fold at the case's stated midpoint assumptions. But that verdict is not robust: MA8 (the Fold's ongoing annual cost, $1,875) is a midpoint of a disclosed $1,095-$2,655 range, and at the top of that same range the Fold's true per-year cost rises to $3,295 -- higher than the Beagle's $2,935.62, flipping the recommendation entirely with no change to any Beagle assumption. The Beagle's Day-1 cost is also $595 lower, leaving a smaller $585 funding gap against the family's $1,620 versus the Fold's $1,180 gap. And the Beagle buys nearly 3 more years of the pet Toby has wanted his whole life -- a raw lifetime-dollar comparison (which most rooms will reach for first) makes the choice look far more lopsided than it actually is per year.
balance.argument_b: The Scottish Fold costs $2,515.00 per year of its expected 10-year life (Day-1 $2,800 + annual $2,235 x 10 years, all divided by 10) -- the cheaper option on the fair, per-year metric, despite a purchase price $500 higher than the Beagle's. The catch: that lower per-year cost is a direct result of a real, documented genetic health condition that shortens the breed's average life by several years -- the same fact that makes the comparison favorable also means Chloe's pick is statistically more likely to need costly veterinary care for a joint disorder, which is exactly what Mom's insurance requirement exists to cover.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = lifetime total cost of ownership (including Mom's required insurance every year) divided by expected lifespan. Option A (Beagle): Day-1 $2,205 (purchase $1,250 + setup $955, MA1/MA2) + annual $2,766 (recurring $2,166 + insurance $600, MA3/MA4) x 13 years (MA5) = lifetime $38,163; per year = $38,163 / 13 = $2,935.62. Option B (Scottish Fold): Day-1 $2,800 (purchase $1,750 + setup $1,050, MA6/MA7) + annual $2,235 (recurring $1,875 + insurance $360, MA8/MA9) x 10 years (MA10) = lifetime $25,150; per year = $25,150 / 10 = $2,515.00. Margin = (2935.62 - 2515.00) / 2515.00 = 16.72%, Option B cheaper per year. The raw, un-normalized lifetime totals ($38,163 vs $25,150, a 51.7% gap) are real, disclosed context and the case's Twist/trap, not the graded primary metric -- see legacy_conversion_note.

Beagle annual insurance premium modeled at $600/year, the midpoint of S1's and S6's cited insurance ranges ($300-$900 and $25-$75/mo respectively, which agree).
Beagle expected lifespan modeled at 13 years, the midpoint of the more commonly cited 12-15-year sub-range within S2's full 10-15-year range, rounded to a whole number.

Scottish Fold purchase price modeled at $1,750, the midpoint of the responsible-breeder, pet-quality tier ($1,000-$2,500, S3) -- chosen over the higher show-quality and 2026 live-marketplace figures since Chloe wants a standard pet-quality kitten, not a show animal.
Scottish Fold one-time setup cost modeled at $1,050, the midpoint of S4's own cited one-time-setup range ($600-$1,500).

Scottish Fold ongoing annual cost (excluding insurance) modeled at $1,875/year, the midpoint of S4's five cited sub-category ranges (food, grooming, medications/vet, environment maintenance, entertainment) summed.
Scottish Fold annual insurance premium modeled at $360/year, directly from S4's cited point figure of $30/month -- no range to take a midpoint of.

Scottish Fold expected lifespan modeled at 10 years -- deliberately the breed-WIDE average from S5, not the higher healthy-individual figure (13-16 years), because the breed-wide average is the real, documented figure that already accounts for the breed's genetic joint condition.

sensitivity_note: The primary metric's 16.72% margin is real but NOT robust to a full +/-50% sweep of the case's own stated assumption dials (case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5, run 2026-08-20, sensitivity_model.py FLEX list) -- the verdict is UNSTABLE under two of the nine: a -50% flex on annual_noins_a_usd (Beagle's ongoing annual cost) or a +50% flex on annual_noins_b_usd (Scottish Fold's ongoing annual cost) both flip the winner from B (cat) to A (dog), and six of the nine dials' +/-50% extremes push the margin outside SPEC section 2's 20% cap (annual_noins_a_usd, annual_noins_b_usd, insurance_a_usd, lifespan_a_years, lifespan_b_years, purchase_b_usd -- range observed 20.9% to 86.1%). This is disclosed explicitly in sensitivity_disclosure[] (all Category F, per-dial), per Tier 2 probe 5's own requirement, rather than left for a guide to discover live: the 16.72% figure is a real, current best estimate anchored to cited sources, not a robust result, and the ongoing-annual-cost dials (MA3/MA8) are the two a discussion should treat as most fragile. See sensitivity_model.py and FACILITATOR.md's Twist section.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: A Beagle's real year-to-year cost of food, grooming, and routine vet care cannot be pinned to one exact dollar figure in advance -- it depends on the specific animal's health, appetite, and activity level, none of which are knowable before the pet is chosen. The case anchors the estimate to the midpoint of two independently corroborating cited sources (S1, S6), a defensible forecast basis, not a guess.

Same forecast-shaped uncertainty as annual_noins_a_usd, for the Scottish Fold: real ongoing cost varies by the individual animal and cannot be known exactly in advance. Anchored to the midpoint of S4's own five cited sub-category ranges.

Real pet insurance premiums vary by underwriter, coverage tier, and the specific dog's age/health at enrollment -- a family choosing a plan next year cannot know today's exact quote. Anchored to the midpoint of two independently corroborating cited premium ranges (S1, S6).

No individual animal's actual lifespan can be known in advance by any amount of research -- this is genuinely irreducible uncertainty, the same category as a future price. The case anchors its estimate to the commonly-cited midpoint of a real, sourced breed-average range (S2), not an invented number.

Same irreducible per-animal uncertainty as lifespan_a_years. The case deliberately uses the real breed-WIDE average (not the higher healthy-individual figure) from S5, which already reflects the documented health condition -- but any single real Scottish Fold could still live a materially different number of years.

A breeder's actual asking price for a specific future kitten cannot be known exactly in advance -- it depends on the individual breeder, litter, and market conditions at the time of purchase. Anchored to the midpoint of the responsible-breeder, pet-quality tier from S3, deliberately excluding the higher show-quality and inflated 2026 live-marketplace listings the same source also reports.
